Murmur
MUR-mur
v. / n.
Latin murmurare, to mutter or rumble—an imitative word, the sound of a low continuous complaint. The form itself is the definition: not a shout, but a grumble passed along under the breath.

Biblical Definition

Murmuring is low, spreading complaint against God's provision and against the leaders He appointed, and Scripture treats it as one of the gravest and most contagious sins of the covenant people. Its home is the wilderness: the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Exod 16:2)—days after the Red Sea, over bread. God hears it as directed at Himself: How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, which murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel (Num 14:27). The murmur is aimed at Moses; God receives the invoice. Paul makes the wilderness a standing warning to the church: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Cor 10:10). And the positive command is stark in its scope: Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Phil 2:14)—all things, which leaves no exempt category of grievance. Jude describes the ungodly as murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts (Jude 16). Two distinctions keep this from becoming cruelty. Murmuring is not lament: the Psalms complain loudly and directly to God, and that is faith speaking. Murmuring is not the lawful bringing of a real grievance to those responsible, as in Acts 6 where a genuine murmuring over neglected widows is answered by structural remedy rather than rebuke. Murmuring is complaint that travels sideways—never to God, never to the man who could fix it, always to the man who cannot.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MURMUR as a low sound continued or continually repeated; and as a complaint half suppressed or uttered in a low muttering voice—grumbling, expressed discontent.

expand to see more

MURMUR, n. — A low sound continued or continually repeated, as that of a stream running in a stony channel, or that of flame.

MURMUR, v.i. — To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice; to utter sullen discontent. The people murmured against Moses (Exod 15:24).

Key Scripture

Exodus 16:2 — "And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness:"

Numbers 14:27 — "How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, which murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against me."

1 Corinthians 10:10 — "Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer."

Philippians 2:14 — "Do all things without murmurings and disputings:"

Modern Corruption

Murmuring has been rebranded as authenticity—venting, processing out loud, speaking one's truth—so that the precise sin Scripture says destroyed a generation now presents itself as honesty and even as courage.

expand to see more

The modern reclassification is nearly total. Sustained sideways complaint is called venting, processing, speaking up, or being real, and the man who does it is praised for not bottling things up. Scripture's category is narrower and more searching. Murmuring is not defined by volume or by emotion but by direction: it goes sideways rather than upward or forward. Israel's complaint was factually accurate—there was no bread—and God still called it evil, because the accurate grievance was carried to everyone except the One who had just parted a sea.

The church must guard the opposite ditch as well. Some leaders use murmuring as a muzzle, labeling any criticism as rebellion and any question as Korah. Acts 6 refutes that outright: a real murmuring over neglected Hellenist widows is met not with a sermon on grumbling but with seven men appointed to fix the neglect. And the Psalms are full of complaint so raw it embarrasses modern piety—addressed to God, which is what makes it prayer instead of murmuring. The test is not whether a man has a grievance. It is where he takes it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lun, to murmur or grumble, the wilderness word; Greek gogguzō, an onomatopoeic verb for muttering—the sound of complaint moving through a crowd.

expand to see more

Hebrew lun (H3885) — to murmur, grumble, complain; the characteristic verb of the wilderness generation (Exod 15:24; 16:2; Num 14:2, 27).

Greek gogguzō (G1111) — to mutter, murmur, grumble in a low tone; used of the Jews murmuring at Christ's words and of the church's forbidden complaining (John 6:41; 1 Cor 10:10; Phil 2:14).

Greek goggusmos (G1112) — a murmuring, secret displeasure; including the lawful grievance of Acts 6:1 that was answered by remedy (John 7:12; Acts 6:1; 1 Pet 4:9).

Usage

"I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel—aimed at Moses; received by God."

"Do all things without murmurings and disputings—Philippians leaves no exempt grievance."

"Lament goes up to God; murmuring goes sideways to the man who cannot fix it."
